title: Fire in my bones (Jeremiah 20:7–9)
hookLine: Jeremiah tries to stop speaking, but the word is "as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones"
carry: silence turned out to be impossible
tomorrow: Seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4–7)

cards: Jeremiah has a bad night. Pashhur, a priest and an officer in the Temple, hears him prophesying disaster, has him struck, and locks him overnight in the stocks at the upper gate of Benjamin, by the house of the Lord.
The next morning Pashhur lets him out, and Jeremiah speaks one more hard word to him. Then the book opens the door to Jeremiah's private prayer, and what comes out is a complaint against God.

teach.b: Here's how it starts. "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me."
The Hebrew verb behind deceived can also mean persuaded or enticed, and translators wrestle with how strong to make it. Either way, Jeremiah is saying: you talked me into this, and I lost.
Every time I open my mouth it's violence and ruin, and every time, I'm laughed at. So he decides to stop.

teach.h: I WILL NOT SPEAK ANY MORE.
teach.b: "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name." And here's what happens.

teach.h: A BURNING FIRE SHUT UP IN MY BONES.
teach.b: "But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay."
Holding it in wears him out more than the mockery did. The word won't stay buried. Two things are worth keeping.

First, the book keeps this prayer. It doesn't tidy Jeremiah into a calm saint. Jewish tradition has room for arguing with God: Abraham bargains over Sodom, Job demands an answer, and here a prophet says, you tricked me.
Second, the fire isn't a reward or a glow of inspiration. It's a pressure. Some truths, once you know them, cost more to keep silent than to say.
Jeremiah's lesson isn't that speaking got easier. It's that silence turned out to be impossible.

how: Jews read Jeremiah's complaints, like this one in chapter 20, as part of the prophetic books; arguing with God, from Abraham to Job to Jeremiah, has a recognized place in Jewish prayer and study.

games.q: you're Jeremiah, mocked every day for what you say. you decide: I won't speak in his name anymore. what happens?
o: the word burns like fire shut up in your bones.
games.why: his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones: holding it in wore him out.

practice: Ask yourself whether there's something you keep swallowing: a truth someone needs to hear, an apology you owe, a worry about someone you love.
Put it into one clear sentence in your head, kind and true, without speaking it to anyone yet. If the sentence comes out angry, breathe and try again until it's honest without being cruel.
